Hi Irene — thanks again for the demo earlier today. Quick recap plus a few clarifying questions our security/compliance team asked to move us toward procurement. Can you confirm the following at a high level (we can do a technical deep dive after):

1) Prompt/output storage: when a user submits text to the API, is the full prompt or the model output ever persisted on Redwood-hosted storage by default? If so, where (region), for how long, and under what conditions is it retained?

2) Telemetry and logs: what gets logged for debugging and performance? Do you keep token-level data in logs (raw text), or is it hashed/redacted? How long are those logs kept?

3) Data residency and encryption: can we keep all stored artifacts (logs, attachments, optional transcripts) inside a US-only region and use our KMS?

4) Opt-out controls: can Luma opt out of prompt retention for our org (we want to ensure no PII is stored)? If opt-out, how does that affect billing/usage visibility and troubleshooting?

5) Evidence: can you share a SOC2 summary and the standard DPA clause around processing of customer-provided content?

Appreciate short, actionable answers — our security team will triage and come back with any follow-ups.

—Sam

Hi Sam — great to meet you all today. Short answers below, and I9ve looped Marissa (Security) and Dev (Engineering) for specifics. I9m attaching a one-pager and our SOC2 summary for initial review.

Summary answers (high level):
- Default behavior: hosted Redwood API does not persist full prompt/response text to long-term customer-visible storage by default. Ephemeral runtime buffers are used for inference and cleared after request completion.
- Optional retention: customers can opt in to store transcripts / full logs for debugging, evals, or auditing; that data is then stored according to a contract-selected region and TTL.
- Telemetry/logging: we capture aggregated usage (token counts, model id, latency) for billing and performance. Debug logs that include request text are only enabled when a customer opts in or opens a support ticket and explicitly approves log capture.
- Residency & encryption: enterprise accounts can require US-only residency and bring-your-own-KMS (BYOK) for stored artifacts.
- Opt-out implications: disabling text retention preserves privacy but limits our ability to debug user-reported misbehavior; billing still works via aggregated token counters.

Next steps: Marissa will provide the security-oriented details (retention windows, redaction rules, audit log retention). Dev can walk through runtime telemetry semantics if you want a technical deep dive. I9ve attached: redwood-data-handling-one-pager.pdf and SOC2-summary-2027.pdf.

If you can send over any short checklist items your team needs (e.g., encryption algorithms, retention windows), we9ll produce a one-page matrix.

Hi Sam — thanks for the clear list. Below are concrete, security-oriented answers you can share with your compliance team. I9m keeping this concise; we can expand into a formal matrix if you prefer.

1) Prompt/output persistence (hosted):
- By default: full prompt and model output are not written to customer-accessible object storage or databases after inference. The runtime keeps ephemeral memory (in-RAM, per-request) only for the duration of the request.
- Opt-in retention: if a customer enables "session transcript" or explicitly requests support log capture, we will persist the full request/response to encrypted object storage. Default opt-in TTL is 30 days in hosted plans; enterprise contracts can set custom TTLs (30 days minimum for auditability, up to multi-year under contract).
- Aggregated billing records: we persist aggregated token counts and model identifiers for billing and quota, with pseudonymized request IDs. Aggregated billing records retain for 13 months by default.

2) Telemetry & debugging logs:
- Performance telemetry (latency, GPU utilization, kernel errors) is stored as numeric metrics and never contains raw prompt text.
- Debug logs that contain textual input/output are off by default. When enabled (customer opt-in or support capture), textual logs are redacted with configurable policies:
  * Full redaction: remove sequences matching configurable sensitive-field patterns (PII regex)
  * Hashing: option to store SHA256 hashes of prompt strings (allows dedup without plaintext storage)
- Log retention for debug captures follows the same TTL as transcripts (30 days default). Audit logs (who accessed what artifact) are retained 24 months for enterprise customers.

3) Data residency & encryption:
- Region control: enterprise and Dedicated customers can restrict where persisted artifacts live (US, EU, APAC) and we support isolated VPC deployments for Private customers.
- Encryption: all persisted artifacts encrypted at rest with AES-256. Enterprise can BYOK via supported KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) — keys remain customer-controlled.

4) Opt-out controls and impact:
- Organization-level opt-out: yes. We provide an org-level setting to disable textual retention. When set, no textual request/response will be written to storage; temporary runtime buffers are still used in memory for inference only.
- Impact: limits our ability to reproduce issues; support workflows will rely on request IDs and aggregated metrics instead. We offer an alternative: on-demand short-lived log capture where the customer temporarily permits capture for a specific support case and then revokes it.

5) Evidence & DPA:
- I attached our SOC2 summary already. The standard DPA clause for processing customer content is at: https://redwood-internal.storage/srv/dpa-luma-health-v1 (shared link above). We can insert narrow clauses for retention TTL and residency in the contract.

Attachments: none in this message (see Irene's attachments).

If you want, we can provision a short-term staging account with retention disabled so your team can run a data-flow test and validate no persisted artifacts are generated.

Hey Sam / team — adding a few runtime-level clarifications from engineering so you9re not surprised in the deep dive: 

- Runtime buffers: the model server keeps KV caches and token buffers in memory per connection. Those buffers are cleared on request completion and are not flushed to disk under normal operation.
- Short-lived traces: lightweight per-request telemetry (request-id, model variant, sequence-length, latency, GPU kernel metrics) is emitted to our metrics pipeline; that data is numeric/metadata only and does not include plaintext tokens.
- Support capture flow: when a customer triggers a support capture we generate a one-time signed capture token that allows log persistence for up to N minutes; the capture is retained per the TTL assigned to the capture (default 30 days).
- Tokenization: we never persist token-level plaintext in persistent logs unless capture is enabled. For customers that require cryptographic proofs we can store secure hashes (SHA256) of requests to allow integrity checks without storing plaintext.
- Config flags (example):
  * retention.default_ttl_days = 30
  * retention.allow_text_capture = false (org-level)
  * telemetry.metrics_retention_days = 400

If you9d like a short technical session, I can walk your infra/security folks through a live demo of a capture flow and show how keys and retention are enforced end-to-end.

—Dev Patel
